turns.doctor_question: Hi, it's good to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, yeah, it's good to meet you too. So, um, I guess the main thing... well, it's been building up for a while, honestly. I work as an insurance claims clerk, so it's a lot of desk work. You know, processing policies, staring at dual monitors, cross-referencing policy numbers, making sure the coverage dates match up with the incident reports. It's tedious, but it pays the bills, and since I didn't finish college, it's a pretty decent gig for me right now. 

But the main thing that finally pushed me to actually make this appointment and come in today is that I just keep getting up from my workstation during the day. Like, constantly. And I know I’m supposed to stay put. I have a quota of claim reviews I need to finish by the end of my shift, and every time I sit down, I tell myself, 'Okay, just power through this batch.' But then, I don't know, a few minutes later I'm up again. I'll go to the breakroom to get water, or I'll walk over to the printer even if I didn't actually print anything, or I'll just stand up to stretch and end up wandering down the hall. It's like my legs just decide they're done sitting. My supervisor walked by yesterday and I wasn't at my desk again, and I could tell she was annoyed. I just sit there, knowing I absolutely need to finish these reviews, and I still just get up and walk away. It's getting to be a real problem.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states they constantly get up from their workstation during the day despite knowing they are supposed to stay seated to finish their work.

turns.doctor_question: When you’re sitting at your desk, do you get an uncomfortable feeling in your legs that makes you feel like you have to move them?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, it’s not really... it’s not like a pain or a creepy-crawly feeling in my legs, if that’s what you mean. It’s not uncomfortable like my muscles ache or anything like that. It’s more just... I don't know, this constant restless energy? Like, even when I am forcing myself to stay in the chair, I’m not actually sitting still. 

For example, we have these quarterly compliance trainings, right? And they are just absolutely brutal. They put us in this stuffy conference room on the second floor, and the chairs are those cheap mesh ones that squeak if you move too much. And I swear, in those trainings or during our longer team meetings—like the ones where the managers just drone on about new underwriting guidelines for what feels like hours—I’m usually bouncing my leg the entire time. Like, my heel is just going up and down, a mile a minute. I don't even realize I'm doing it until the person next to me gives me a look because I'm shaking the whole table. 

And if I try to stop the leg bouncing, like if I really force myself to keep both feet flat on the floor, I just end up doing something else. I'll start clicking my pen. I actually had to switch to using those cheap pens with the caps instead of the retractable ones because my coworker got so annoyed with me clicking it during a presentation last month. Or I'll just be constantly shifting around in the chair, crossing my legs, uncrossing them, leaning forward, leaning back. And the whole time, I'm genuinely trying to look focused! I'm staring right at the speaker, nodding, trying to look like the perfect employee who is absorbing every single word about the new policy updates, but my body just refuses to stay at rest. It's just this constant need to be doing something with my hands or my feet, even when I'm trying my hardest to just be normal and sit there.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly describes bouncing their leg, clicking their pen, and constantly shifting or squirming in their chair during meetings.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes experiencing a 'constant restless energy' and feeling that their body 'refuses to stay at rest'.

turns.doctor_question: Were you already this fidgety and unable to stay seated when you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, actually, looking back... it really isn't a new thing at all. It's funny you ask about when I was a kid, because my mom actually kept a bunch of my old report cards and parent-teacher conference notes in this big plastic bin in her attic, and I was looking through them a couple of years ago when I was helping her move. And, man, it was like reading a script of my life right now, just scaled down to a third-grade level. 

Like, my teachers would always write these really specific notes. They'd say things like, "He's a very bright boy, very capable," which was always nice, but then there was always a "but." It was always, "but he loses his worksheets constantly." And it was true! I remember having this red folder that was supposed to be for homework, and somehow the papers would just vanish between my desk and my backpack. Or they'd say I missed instructions. Like, the teacher would stand at the front of the room, explain exactly how to do the diorama project or the math assignment, and I’d just be sitting there... maybe looking out the window, maybe drawing on my desk, and then suddenly everyone is working and I have absolutely no idea what we're supposed to be doing. 

And the reminders... oh man. They were always saying I needed constant reminders to actually finish my classwork. I'd start a worksheet, get through maybe the first three questions, and then I'd just drift off. I'd start organizing my crayons, or I'd be trying to see what the kid next to me was doing, or I'd just be staring into space thinking about a video game. The teacher would have to come tap on my desk and say, "Focus, we need to finish this before recess." So, yeah, the fidgeting and the not staying on task... it's definitely been there since elementary school. It's just that back then, the consequence was missing five minutes of recess, and now the consequence is my supervisor glaring at me because I haven't processed enough insurance claims. But the underlying feeling? The getting distracted and needing someone to basically herd me back to what I'm supposed to be doing? That's been happening for as long as I can remember.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes drifting off after only a few questions on a worksheet and being unable to stay on task.
symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient mentions not absorbing instructions when the teacher was speaking directly to the class, instead looking out the window and having no idea what to do.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient explicitly states they missed instructions and needed constant reminders to finish their classwork.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient recalls constantly losing worksheets and having homework papers vanish from their folder.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes getting distracted by things like looking out the window, drawing on the desk, or watching the kid next to them.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient confirms the doctor's question about fidgeting, stating that the fidgeting has definitely been there since elementary school.

turns.doctor_question: Do you ever feel driven to repeat certain behaviors—like checking, counting, arranging, or washing—even when you know they don’t really make sense?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, sure, I have to double-check my work sometimes, right? Like with the claims, if I’m entering a policy number, I might look back at the source document just to make absolutely sure I didn’t transpose a 7 and a 9, because doing that messes up the whole system and then the adjusters get mad. But that’s just, you know, normal job stuff. It’s not like I feel this intense, overwhelming urge to do it over and over again until it feels "just right" or anything like that. 

I don't really have any weird rituals or anything. Like, I don't need to tap the doorframe three times before I leave a room, and I'm definitely not a germaphobe. My apartment is actually a bit of a mess, to be honest. I mean, my desk at work is pretty cluttered too, with sticky notes and half-empty coffee cups. I definitely don't spend time arranging things perfectly. If anything, my problem is the exact opposite—I can't seem to keep things organized or stick to a routine to save my life. So, no, I don't get those urges to repeat things or wash my hands constantly or anything like what you're describing. It's really just the distraction and the restless energy that are the main issues for me.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient states they cannot keep things organized and describes their apartment and desk as messy and cluttered.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly identifies distraction as one of their main issues.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly identifies restless energy as one of their main issues.
symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient explicitly denies having urges to repeat behaviors, perform rituals, arrange things perfectly, or wash hands constantly.
